title: Mitchell Hashimoto’s new way of writing code
summary: Mitchell Hashimoto on HashiCorp's history, AI-driven pressure on open source and Git, and his habit of always keeping an agent working on planning, research or code.

assertions.quote: AI makes it trivial to create plausible-looking but incorrect and low-quality contributions

verdicts.note: Maintainers of curl, Ghostty and others document floods of low-effort AI PRs and reports, and GitHub added tooling to restrict PRs in response.

assertions.quote: Git and GitHub uh forges in their current form do not work with agentic infrastructure today

verdicts.note: Merge-queue and monorepo strain is reported by heavy agent users, but the evidence is anecdotal and Git scales far with existing extensions.

assertions.quote: I endeavor to always have an agent doing something at all times.

verdicts.note: Plausible for research-style tasks, but no study measures the net gain against review and context-switching costs.

METR Feb 2026: developers using agentic tools often worked on unrelated tasks while waiting, and some ran several agents at once, which made per-task time unreliable. The practice is common, but the extra output is not measured.

assertions.quote: I absolutely love them for research.

verdicts.note: Agents speed up broad searches and surveys, but deep-research outputs still contain errors and fabricated details that need checking.

assertions.quote: Oh, if I do a separate planning step, it does so much better.

verdicts.note: Plan-then-execute consistently reduces agent rework in practice and in vendor evals, especially on multi-file tasks.

assertions.quote: Oh, if I have a better test harness for it to execute, it does a lot better.

verdicts.note: Agent benchmarks and practice consistently show verifiable feedback (tests, compilers) is the main driver of agent success.

assertions.quote: oh if it makes a mistake and I add that just to agents.md, it never makes that mistake again.

verdicts.note: Encoding lessons in rules and workflows does reduce repeat mistakes, but rule files bloat and conflict if not pruned; gains are real but not automatically compounding.

assertions.quote: it takes much longer than an hour to get proficient with git, but you put in the effort and then you reap the rewards later.

verdicts.note: Learning curves are real (METR's one dev with >50h Cursor experience was faster), but evidence that ramp-up reliably flips results is thin.

assertions.quote: when it turns into productionizing something, uh it feels similar to what it's always been.

verdicts.note: Direction is well supported: greenfield, low-stakes work gets the biggest gains in studies and surveys. The specific multipliers are anecdote.

assertions.quote: I would much rather someone just like throw slop at a wall that you're never going to ship

verdicts.note: Validating demand before building is long-standing product practice; AI lowers prototype cost, making it more attractive.

assertions.quote: I think if you use the tools wrong, you do think less

verdicts.note: Anthropic's 2026 RCT found AI-assisted learners scored lower on mastery of a new library, and other studies show reduced engagement; effects depend on how AI is used.
